segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, yeah, we knew him very well. In fact, I worked for him. He had a Samovich. You know Scandinavians, they always turn the V's and the W's around. Well, it's Sam Samovich was his name.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was he like?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, he was like, like old Arthur said, he was a real nice fellow and he could hardly speak English so you could understand him. And he was a boss for the Potlatch. And he had a fellow that worked in his crew that was just real troublesome and quarrelsome and always quarreling with the men. And so he fired him one day and the old Sam had a shovel on his shoulder and he walked up to this fellow and told him that he had a double-bitted axe and he hit it Sam with that axe and hit the shovel and just come right down through his arm until his arm just barely hung on. You know, just all to cut it off. And so, but they fixed it back so that he could use it. So, and then he was section boss there for years and years. Arthur told me that story, told me something like that. He told me that Sam shot the guy. And he shot him and killed him.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, he had a pistol. He had a pistol and when the fellow cut his arm off of the axe, well he just shot him and killed him right there. So that's what happened then. Yeah. That's what happened. He said something that Sam had just gotten that pistol back from T .P. Jones. T .P. had it barred in front of him. Anyway, he happened to have it in his pocket. And he said he just emptied it right into him. He said, he said, I shot every shell I had. He said, if I had more, I'd have shot more. I think Arthur said something like, I shot him once and he kept coming. I shot him twice. He kept coming. I shot him three times and he went down like a sober man. But I remembered that that old fella, he was, he was, you're a nice old guy.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did you come from?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: I'm coming to some house. I'll be sure to get someone.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Of course, I was just, just a boy, 15, 16. I guess I was 16 then. In the summer I worked there and there was a couple other boys who worked there. And the track that went out from that camp, we went over a lot of hilly ground, uphill and downhill and in the low places, the track would sink in the mud. So we, we had to split rails, just like they do fence rails, and jack the track up in low places and put those rails underneath the track. Well, it seemed like we always found the best timber up on top of the hills and he had a, you know, we had an old push car and we'd load those rails on the push car and take them down to the bottom. And old Sam had a hole cut in the, in the floor of the car. Then he had a Peavey stalk, old broken Peavey stalk and he tapered so that he could stick it down in there and use it for brake. And about once every two or three days we'd manage to cover up the hole on that push car so he couldn't get that stick in there. And then when we'd get it loaded, he'd jump on and we'd give him up. He couldn't get the thing brakes. Down the hill he would go, you know. And when he'd get to the bottom, he'd jump off and he'd shake his fist out. He knew we did it on purpose. Then he'd watch us like everything for a day or two, you know, and then he'd forget again. Oh, we used to have a lot of fun with him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How big was the crew that you guys had working?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: We only had about six or seven men, about six or seven men. Another thing we used to do, we used to hunt bee trees. We're supposed to be working and we'd hunt bee trees. And he didn't have any use for the honey. He boarded in the camp, you know. There was a man who worked on the crew that lived at home and he didn't live very far from the camp. And so we'd just hunt bee trees. He'd send two of us at a time, go and hunt bee trees. When we'd find a bee tree, the whole crew would go and cut it and give the honey to that man that worked there. And he didn't have any use for it himself, but he just wanted to make a good fellow out of himself, I guess. I don't know. That sounds like he wasn't too hard on you. Oh no, oh no, no. He used to tell us, now boys, he said, I don't care whether you work or not, but he said, don't sit down and keep your tools in your hands. He said, I don't care whether you work or not. I sure got a chuckle out of this when I see what Arthur had to say about old Sam Samovich.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, he'd been there for some years when you went to work for him, right?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, yes. It had been some time before that he had his arm cut. Because it was all healed up until he could use it, but he wouldn't let any of the Potlatch bosses know that he could use it. He'd walk around when they were around, he'd walk around that arm and just go like this. But he could use it pretty good if he wanted to do it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that how he got to be a boss?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: He was a boss before. That just ensured him his job, you see, because he'd got hurt there on the job. Because he got hurt, they would keep him. They'd keep him on. And he knew that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This guy who got in a fight with and killed, he's just a troublemaker?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, that's what they said. Said he was just a sort of a troublemaker, always quarreling with the other men in the crews. And he was just a sort of a troublemaker.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you go after the bees in those days?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, you find where the bees water generally. They'll water the closest water from the tree. And then you can watch them. They go in a straight line. See, from that water hole, they'll just raise and go in a straight line towards that tree. And when they fill up with water, while they're heavy and they fly slow, you can just watch one and just tell exactly what direction he goes. And then follow him. And then if it's too far, then you can look at the trees and kind of figure which tree is a bee tree, if it looks like it's hollow, got holes in it or anything. Or else you had a bee box with some little honey or honeycomb in it. And you'd follow that bee as far as you could see him and then set this box down. And then they'd start working that honey. And then you'd get another line on them and tell you you could find the tree.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you trap them in the box once they went inside it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, sometimes. Sometimes some of them had a little glass lid on the box and they'd get three or four bees in there. And then they'd watch one go and then they'd put this glass lid over. And they'd watch one as far as they could go. And they'd pick the box up and go and set it down there. And then they'd let out another one and watch that one. And it wouldn't take too long. You could find the tree. And there were just lots and lots of bees in that country. Oh, that was out on that ridge. It'd be south of where Arthur lives there. There were just worlds of bees in there that year.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: After you find the bee tree, then what? Then you go and you get a bunch of guys who'll cut it down?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Then they'd just cut it down and cut the chunk right out where the bees were and split it and get the honey out. If the bees didn't sting you so much, you had to leave first.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What'd you do to stop that from getting stung?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, sometimes they'd wait until night to cut the section out and get the bees out. But some people now, they don't seem to bother much. And they'd go right in there and cut the section out and get the honey and the bees just swarm all around them. That's not for me. They really went after me.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When they cut the section out, would they make the honey right there? What would they do with the honey after they cut it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Just put it in the pail and just take it out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You didn't boil it or anything?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, no. It was right in a comb. You can just pick the combs right out and put them in pails. It is good just the way it came out of the tree.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you mark the tree? Would you mark the tree once you found it so you could find it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, some of them used to. Some of them would mark the tree and then it was supposed to be theirs. No one else was supposed to cut it. But like we were there, we would just follow them as soon as we found them and take the honey.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, when was it that you were working on the crew for Sands?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: That was in 1918. 1918, First World War.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you working the 10-hour days?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, that was eight-hour days, six days a week. I hadn't gotten down to the five-day week yet at that time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you bunk in the camp then?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, yes. When I first went to work there, everyone had to carry his own bed. During that summer is when the company started furnishing beds for the men. Before that time, everybody had to furnish their own bed. Every old lumberjack had a bedroll and he'd roll it up and when he'd go from one camp to the other, he'd roll that bedroll up and take down the railroad track a foot, you know, to the next camp.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember, were you ever in a camp before they improved those conditions?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, yes… when I first started, you had to carry your own bed. You had an old bunk made out of just rough 1x12s and a little straw in there and you just rolled your blankets out on that. That's where you slept… bed bugs… oh, you can't imagine. Of course, we didn't have any running water. Every bunkhouse had a water pail and a wash stand in the corner where you'd carry your own drinking water and use that old tin wash basin. And you had to keep a newspaper over the water bucket to keep the bed bugs out of it. They'd fall down from the ceiling in the water pail. I'm glad I wasn't there. Men just lived with that… oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You just had to take that for a good job.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: In the summertime, a lot of people just take their blankets and move out underneath the trees, get away from the bed bugs out of those old bunkhouses.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You might tell them how they fed you too out there.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Hmm?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You might tell them how they fed you out there. Bunch of houses with yellow jackets and that.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I worked in one camp where they hauled a lunch out to us at noon with a team and a wagon. It was supposed to be a hot lunch. They'd have a big round can full of potatoes and another one full of meat and another one full of gravy and so on. It'd be hot when they'd leave the camp, but it wouldn't be a very hot time. They'd get to the woods with it. They had a great big tent that they were supposed to use to eat lunch in. They had tables in there. The yellow jackets were so thick that you just couldn't eat any meat. When that team would come in there, somebody would grab that can of meat and just start out through the woods and just scatter it out there and let the yellow jackets have that. You couldn't eat any meat. That's all there was to it. They were just in clouds. The same way with that tent, you couldn't eat in there because it was just thick in there with it. Everybody'd get their plate filled and then just take to the woods and get out of away from that campground a little ways and try to eat. That sounds like an awful tough working situation. Oh yeah. It's one thing to hear talk about low wages, but it's another thing to talk about a place where you can barely stand in conditions. That was low wages too. We got 50 cents an hour then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've heard somebody told me once that they had a vial of mercury in it that they thought would protect them. No, I never knew of any. I never knew of any.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: I don't think they ever got rid of those until they got the DDT.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I remember how they used to strip the under clothes off and throw it against the wall and if it stuck then it changed them. It was time for a bath.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah. I don't think somebody's pulling your leg when they're tying you around.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: There's one old fella in one camp I worked at and he had lice. So every morning he'd pull his undershirt off and turn it wrong side out and put it back on. He said, I have to work for a living. He said, those so-and-so lice can do the same.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What would you do when you were in a camp with no place to wash or anything? How would you cope with them bed bugs?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, you just endured them. That was all. You just had a little old tin wash basin and that was it. You know, you carried your own water maybe from the creek or from the source that they had for the cookhouse. The first camps had no running water at all. Then later they nearly always had running water after a few years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get to come home very often?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, well, you had to walk. There was no transportation. I worked in camps up the other side of Helmer and Saturday night after supper while you just start down the railroad track and walk down here after work Saturday night and then walk back Sunday night and think nothing of it. Now then that would be quite a journey, you know. You probably got to clean up when you got home. Oh yes, yeah. You'd come home Saturday nights and get cleaned up and clean clothes and whatnot and then go back again. But in the wintertime, of course, you didn't always get home every week. There'd be too much snow, hard walking, and you wouldn't make it every week.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was Sam, Samovich different from most of the foremen in not not expecting too much of his crew?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, yes he was. He was different than most of the foremen in that way. But of course, you see, he only had a real small crew and the didn't have anything to do with the actual logging. He was just keeping up the railroad.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the other guys in the crew like you? Were they local boys?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, they were all local boys that worked there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, I was going to ask you, did the IWWs have much to do with this improving of conditions when you were in the camp?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, that was, I think, the beginning of it. The IWWs, that was the, I think, really the kind of a forerunner of the labor unions. And they had a lot to do, I think, cleaning up those camps and furnishing the beds for the men and so on. I think they had a lot to do with that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you hear about them when you were working in the woods? Did you hear about the IWWs?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yes, yeah, we heard a lot about them. But they didn't bother any around this part of the country as far as the timber work was concerned. But they did most of their damage in the farming areas and the thrashing machines. They're supposed to have burned up several thrashing machines and things like that. But the Potlatch had an organization that you had to join in order to work for them. They called them the Loyal Legion of Loggers and Lumbermen, 4Ls. And when you went to camp and got a job, you had to join the 4Ls and they give you a button with 4Ls on it. And you had to wear that button to show that you were a loyal citizen.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did the men buy that pretty much? Did they believe it or did they just do it to go along?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, they just went along with it. In order to get a job, they just went along with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think a lot of those guys belonged to the Wobblies?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I don't think very many of them that worked in the woods. In these camps up here, there were very, few because there was never any trouble around here that I know of. That's sure a good picture of old Arthur, isn't it? Yeah, it really is.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I went and visited him that day after I stopped to see you. I read him this book, but he hadn't seen it. So I went over and read it. Would you tell me again about how your grandfather came into this country?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, well, he came from Indiana. I think he had some relatives that lived over here at Marshall, Washington. Anyway, that's where they spent the first winter. Then they were looking for their homestead. So he came up the Palouse River where these gold miners over the other side of the divide here were mining gold. They had a sort of a road from Colfax up the Palouse River. Then came over the divide this way and located on this little creek over here on Bear Creek. And he told me that... I asked him why he came to this part of the country. I told him, you surely could have found better farmland than up here and this timber. Well, he said there were three things we were looking for. He said we had to have timber to build with and we had to have And then we wanted some open ground that was fairly easy to clear so they could get some land in cultivation. And they found some fairly open timber, almost natural meadows on this little creek. And so that's where they homesteaded. He and his brother-in-law came in here together.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you tell me he was the first man in this country?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, he was the first man in here. He came in in 1884 and there's no other homesteaders here. Then he went back to Marshall and spent the winter and then the next spring he came back and then there was, by that time, there was two or three others in here. And then from then on it settled up real fast.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Whereabouts was, what's the first place that he located here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: It's just about, oh, maybe three miles right straight, almost straight east of here on Bear Creek. Right at the put of those mountains there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And when you say he was the first man in this area, you're talking about from there clear over here and around Avon?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Around the Avon country. And I don't know whether there was anyone around the Deary area then or not. But if there was, there was very, very few.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did he describe, tell you what the country was like when he first came here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, he said there was no underbrush like there is now. And he said that it's all open timber. He said you could just take a team in a wagon and just start out in the general direction you wanted to go and just go there. He said you had to drive around the draws and that was about the only thing. He said you could just drive a team in a wagon right out through the timber anywhere. The Indians evidently kept it burned off. That's what I've always heard. That they kept the underbrush down. And there was nowhere near the game in this country then that there is now because there was no like deer and elk because there was no brush for them to feed on. And that's what they need is the brush.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was your grandfather's name?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Lunsford, Lunsford, James Lunsford.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It seems like he's been here for a long time... What it felt like to be the first man to settle in a country where there's just about nobody else.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I don't know. He never said much about it. He and his brother-in-law came in together and his brother-in-law settled on this little creek over here for Wayne Denisleys. I don't know if you know where Wayne Denisleys is or not but his brother-in-law's homestead was over there on that little creek and my granddad's over on this Bear Creek. Were they fairly close together Oh, they were about four miles apart, I guess. A lot of elbow room. Oh, yeah. But you see for the first few years there was in here there was no no roads. There was a settlement in Moscow at that time but there was no road between and they still went back to Colfax to do their trading and get their mail. But then after the railroad come through, down through Troy, well then they got a road through that way from Troy up to in Bovill. He was later. I don't know just when. There was a town in Kendrick when he came in here. It was after the railroad went through from Kendrick to Moscow before he came in. Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: He built a cabin and a log barn and a log cabin and I don't know how long he lived in the first one and then he built a second house and lived in that for several years and then later on he built the third house. He had he built three different houses on his homestead. And he built a barn in 1906. He built a pretty good-sized barn and then he built his new house after that. Several years after that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he ever talk to you about what it was like getting by in those first first years and how he how he managed it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, not too much. He said they used to hunt game and fish a lot and then after they'd been here a few years, well, they would go back to Colfax to harvest in harvest time and make enough money to live on till the next year, bring back a year supply of groceries and take their team and wagon and go to Colfax and harvest. And I can remember when they'd come back from harvest, his oldest boy is to be my uncle, when he got old enough to take a team, well, they had two teams and they'd go to Colfax and work in the harvest and bring back the whole wagon load full of groceries and flour and whatnot. It lasted a whole year. But they had pretty rough going, I'm sure. Well, I guess I told you about Billy Bowers the time he had the little girl got sick, didn't I? Oh, yeah, well, Billy had, he had had two children by that time. The oldest one was a girl, she was about two years old and then the baby was real small and he'd gone to Colfax to harvest and this girl got real sick. And so Mrs. Bowers left the baby in bed and carried the girl over to the neighbors. It was a sort of a practical nurse and got her to kind of doctor up and then carried her back again. And that day or the day before it had rained in Colfax till they couldn't harvest. So Billy, he'd borrowed a saddle horse and rode home to see how the family was getting along and found out this girl was sick. So he put that horse in the barn and got another one and rode to Troy and got some medicine and rode back and just traded the horses again and started right back for Colfax. You see, there would have been, well, it's 50 miles from here to Colfax. So you see, he rode over, it'd be at least 125 miles without any rest. What were you telling me about how he came into this, when he came into this country, he had a harder role than most people to start going because of the better land had been taken by then. He was one of the last of the homesteaders to start in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that what you were telling me?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, he wasn't too far behind the others, that is, much later than the others. He got pretty good land, only some of it is a little steep up there on the side of Spud Hill, but he wasn't so much later than the others. But they just had real tough going, you know, no way to make any money. My granddad said, as far as money's concerned, he said we didn't need any, we didn't have any place to spend it.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Didn't they pick wild strawberries and can them?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yeah, Mrs. Bauer told me that said the only fruit they had was huckleberries and wild strawberries. They'd been getting that really good. Oh, they're small. Oh yes, they're just real small.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Didn't you say that, didn't you tell me that he, when your grandfather worked for money and know what to do with it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, he said that after he'd been here a couple, three years while a man homesteaded in here and hired him to split some fence rails, he said, and when I got through, he said he paid me money and he said I didn't know what to do with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah. Well, he knew that because all the work they did was exchange.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Just exchange work, you know, and my granddad was a good hunter and the other neighbors would come and work for him and get him to hunt for them, kill them a deer. Yeah, they just, everybody just exchanged work and helped one another. Yeah, it wasn't much different when we came here. That's what 47 years ago when we moved in here. It was just about the same.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: There he is. That's his kids. There's one, another boy. He's supposed to be in there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, he's a distinguished looking fellow. Oh, yes.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: He's a hot fellow. You never get him to laugh aloud. He'd chuckle, you know, but he wouldn't laugh aloud at all. One time they grew corn, little short corn, they had little ears about so big. And I hadn't had corn for a long time and boy, I was really eating corn. And I said, boy, I've eaten a lot of corn. And I looked, here they had a great big pile, but he gathered them up from the rest of the people and put it by my plate, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was it you were telling me about Billy Bowers hunting?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, they'd tell about him in the wintertime. He'd get on a deer track and he'd follow that track until it got to dark that he couldn't see. And he'd just stop under a tree and wait till daylight and keep right on that same track till he run that deer down. Well, it was just a case of have to. They just had to have it almost, you know. Almost had to have it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did Billy have, Billy Bowers had more kids or?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, yes. He had a big family. Yeah, let's see. They had eight kids all together.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it harder for him than for a lot of other people?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I don't know as it was much different. Of course, he had that big family to support, but until they got big enough to work, when those kids got big enough to work, well, they helped, which all the kids had to do. You know, they wouldn't even have school during the time of the year when the kids were needed at home. They would have a split school year. They'd have maybe three months in the winter and in the late spring when the kids could work while they didn't have school.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: I didn't realize he was that much taller than she. I don't even know. Short girl.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They didn't have school at all during the time of working in the field?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, as long as the time of the year when the kids could work in the field while they didn't have school.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was that saying that you were telling me before about living on the farm? One old homesteader said he said, oh, how did he say that?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: He said, yeah, he said, I lived all last winter on fried snowballs and boiled rabbit tracks. Yeah, that sounds pretty tough.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what kind of local industry was it before the railroad came in for a fatherhood?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: It just was none.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: They cut wood didn't they?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, not before the railroad came. There wasn't any. But after they got a road through Detroit, they used to cut wood and haul to Troy to sell the wood. They'd get probably a dollar and a half card for the wood in Troy. And if the roads were good, they could haul about one and a half cards and it would take a day for a man to make that much. So he'd work two days for a dollar and a half.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: What could they do now?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: The first, there was a homesteader homesteaded right south of here and he had the first hay baler in the country and he would bale his hay and store it in the barn and then in the wintertime, he'd want that hay hauled to Troy and he'd pay 50 cents a ton to get that hay hauled to Troy. And my granddad said that he'd just let it be known around the neighborhood that he's ready to haul his hay and anyone wanted to haul, come with their teams and sleds and he said, if you got there in time to get a load, you had to get there way before daylight. They'd just swarm in there to haul that hay for 50 cents a ton near Detroit.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How much hay do you think you could haul on a wagon?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, it'd be on the sled in the wintertime. They'd probably could haul one and a half ton with a team if the roads were broke out pretty good, to make about 75 cents.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was it, was it often pretty tough to get from near Detroit?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, it was awful hilly. You see, they had no way to grade the roads out of the side hill, so they'd just have to go straight up one hill and down the other and there was lots of hills. They did an awful lot of hauling after the railroad got into Troy. And lumber and wood and fence posts and everything like that, baled hay. In the summertime, the dust would be about a foot deep and then the spring in the fall, the mud would be almost hub deep on the wagon.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how do you think a homesteader like your grandfather would have built up his place through the years? Would he have started with just a cow maybe and cleared up just a few acres and then would have grown from there?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, they cleared the land just as fast as they could clear it and got into hay. And cattle the same way. I don't know where he brought his start in. Cattle had to come from down that Colfax country someplace, I suppose. But by the time the railroad came through here in 1906, he had quite a few cattle. And then he butchered beef for the railroad. And he got a pretty good start that way and he got a good market for his cattle.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: And they cleared the land and planted orchards too didn't they?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, they had, every one of these homesteaders had a good orchard. They tried to be as self-sufficient as they could, raise their own gardens and orchards and everything of that kind.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it is for home use?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yeah, all for home use, yeah. I don't think they ever sold anything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was cattle more of a way of making a living for people than crop was or was hay the main crop?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Hay and cattle was the main crops, yeah.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well didn't your granddad raise the hay for the camps too?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yeah, after the Potlatch came in, then there was a good market for Timothy hay for the horses. And he used to sell hay every fall to the Potlatch. So before they came in with the Potlatch, when the Potlatch came in with the railroad, the only market was what you could sell out of Troy and ship from Troy pretty much. Well I don't think there was a, I'm not even sure there was a road through Detroit before the, yes there was. See the railroad went down through Moscow and Troy and Kendrick before there was ever a railroad up through here. And after that railroad went in there, well then they made a road up through to Deary-Bovill. And so they had a market there before there was this railroad came through here. This one came through in 1906. See he'd been here 20 years by that time. So there was a, their first market was down in that country, Troy and Moscow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the community at Avon? When did that start getting going?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well they had a town before the railroad came through. There was another town up the road here about a mile and it was a pretty good sized town. And they had a town there before there was a town in Deary. And then when the railroad came through, they put the station down where Avon is now and then they moved the post office down there where the station was. Then the original town just folded up. But there was a pretty good sized town there before there was ever a town in Deary.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Did they have a bank or anything there? They had a Jewelers' drawer. I remember somebody had that.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: They had a meat market and general store and dance hall and liver stable and a barbershop and a saloon or so. I don't know what all they did have there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This is the old Avon?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: The old Avon.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where is the old Avon located from present Avon?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well it would be just southeast a little. Just southeast of the old Avon about maybe a mile.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Where the cemetery is now...

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is there any record anymore of that?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No buildings left at all anymore. Buildings are all gone and they're farming over the land now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Many people live right in that little town there?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes, there was quite a few houses and quite a few people lived there. In fact, the second Avon, at one time there was 42 people lived there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Or now there's what?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Six. Six there now.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: There used to be a lot more days. One day there's now. There isn't anything there now but they had a store and a post office.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: One time they had two pretty good sized stores there at one time. I see in here a picture of Deary in 1906 about the time the railroad came through. There certainly wasn't much there then.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: What was the name of the station down here? Was that Vassar? The railroad when they came through they named all the little stations along by schools.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Colleges.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Started at Harvard or Princeton, Harvard.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: There was Princeton, Harvard, Wellesley, Yale, Vassar, Cornell. They named the stations all after the colleges.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Avon lost out to Vassar?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, the post office named Avon and the station is called Vassar. But the post office kept the name of Avon. There's supposed to have been the first picture, the first house that was in Avon. It was down, Delbert Byers owns the land now, but I can remember that house. It hasn't been too many years ago since that was torn down.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So Avon was really quite a big drawing place for the country around?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes, it was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there a family on every hundred and sixteen in?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, at one time or another there was. There was a family on just about every quarter section and there were just a lot of people around this country. A lot more than there are now.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Where was the school then?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Where was it? Well, the first school was right over there by where the old church building is now. And when the railroad came through, why the railroad went right beside the schoolhouse. So they tore the or they moved the schoolhouse then on the hill.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: We had two two different rooms in when we came here.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, but at first there was only one. When I started this school there, there's about 45 kids who went to that school in one room, all eight grades and one teacher. You don't know who you feel more sorry for, the kids who teach you. 45 kids and one teacher.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: All the same grade.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I started the school there in 1908 and the teacher that was teaching then just died here about what, two months ago. About two or three months ago, Florence Densmore… do you know?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I know of her though.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: You know of her? She lived in Troy. Her husband had the first service station in Troy, Homer.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you remember about those early years you spent in school there?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I don't know. It was something different than they have now.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You definitely kept her ready to grow in that way.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yes. Boys especially, they had to stay out and work so much, you know, that the time they got through the eighth grade they were grown men, some of them. Had a big old stove and sat in one corner. Real cold days while we all had to move up around the stove. Couldn't eat through with that one stove.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: And the kids all went out and tried to get wet so they could sit with the stove. Where did you take your examinations?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, the kids knew each other a lot better than they did later in the big schools, but it seems to me like that would be a pretty hard situation to figure on learning.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, you see a teacher wouldn't have any time at all to spend with individual kids. The time she would assign lessons for eight grades and hear them all recite their lessons and so on, why the day would be gone. ... Oh yes. The big girls always had to help the teacher. See, they'd correct papers and probably teach through the smaller grades because just one person just couldn't do it all to themselves. No, no, they all spoke English from the time I started the school. Some of their parents couldn't speak English very good, but the kids all could. Great, many of them are Scandinavians around this part of the country, Norwegians and Swedes and Danish. Those folks are hard working as some people say. Oh yes, I'll tell you they worked, especially those people from those Scandinavian countries who were hard workers.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: When they clear off this land by hand, that'd work. We did that too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did they have to clear the land with around here? Was it just a stump puller?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well mainly we didn't have stump pullers. We had an old axe in a grub hole and you'd grubbed out the small ones and farmed around the big ones. They tell about, well not too many years ago, there's a couple of farmers met in town. One of them asked the other one, well he said you about got your crop in and yep, he said almost only got nine stumps left. Just farmed around the stumps until you could burn them out or until they'd rot out.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: It just seems fantastic now to watch them with the dozers and things. That's what all we used to do. The way they'd trash and the way they'd trash nowadays was so different.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I can remember my granddad trashing grain with a flail on the barn floor. He had a big old canvas he laid out on the barn floor and put the grain on there and beat it out with a flail. And take a pitchfork and get the straw and feed the straw to the cattle and he'd have the grain left.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did he do with his grain?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: He'd have some grain to feed his horses when he worked the horses hard while they had to have oats. So he'd trash it out with a flail.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: He thought I'd just hit him with hay and all. He was a real tracer.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well he did the thrashing you see while the horses weren't working hard and they didn't get grain then. And then he had the straw to feed to the cattle.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: When we first came here they put the hay grain in a big stack like this and then they'd come in with a stationary trash can and trashed it out.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When was that that you first came here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: In 1928. 1928. That thrashing machine was still going strong then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember, did you know Joe Wells?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yes.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah. I knew him well. Joe and Chuck and Roy. And Mary.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he have much of a log in operation, Joe?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes, he used to do a log quite a little bit. I think there's a picture of him right in here. There's a picture of Joe and Chuck and Roy and their logging operations. Here's a picture of Joe and his wife. They logged somewhat different then than they do now too with those old horses. They'd take those logs and pile them up there in a pile. Well Joe and Lou had that, they called it a halfway house too right in the early days. Yeah, Joe and his wife were running that. His wife was supposed to be a pretty good cook. That wasn't how they called Mary. No, that was the daughter. Mary was the daughter. And Joe and I think his wife's name was Lou. Yeah, Joe and Lou.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he the one that he and the horse were only fighting in?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: He used to make fun of the Swedes. He said the only difference between a nigger and a Swede, he said the Swede is a nigger turned wrong side out. He said he's black inside. Then after they got the bank in Deary, the old banker's name was Harsh. And Joe he says, you know for a long time me and old man Harsh was the only white folks in Deary. He said all the rest are Swedes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I take it Harsh wasn't a Swede?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, he wasn't a Swede. They say Joe drank a lot too. Yeah, he did. He used to drink quite a little.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Have you ever heard those stories about Joe standing up to old Marshall Hades in Troy?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I've heard stories about Joe Wells and Cougar Jack Sterman, how they used to go on a bender and just about take a town like Troy. They tell a story about a time they went to Troy and they were running their horses up and down the street and shooting their guns in the air. And the old Marshall come out and took a few shots at him. That was at night. And old Joe he was telling about it and he says, the damn old fool didn't know any better than to try to shoot a nigger after dark. He says.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.timestamp: 01:08:41"Sound like Joe didn't mind poking fun at his own color or anybody else."

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well everybody accepted him just like they were fighting.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: That's what I've heard. They were real well liked. They were.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Accepted.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And as Mary Wells, when we first came here with the other kid, she said, you don't think I have any white skin do you?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: She showed me her hands, all her hands are white. And she sold her feet. She took her shoes off and sold them to her feet. She used to make cookies for us all the time. My dad worked in Kansas. She kind of worked with my dad when he first went to work there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was she the first black person that you'd known?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well I kind of think she was the first one I'd known.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well they were the first Negroes that I ever saw. As far as I know they were the only Negroes in this part of the country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was Joe really a strong man?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well I don't know if he was very strong. He wasn't very big. He wasn't what you'd call a big man. I've been told that he was. A lot of people told me that it was Chuck that was an especially strong fellow. Chuck of course was a lot bigger than his dad. I don't know how they would work for strength but Joe really wasn't a big man. Well his Cougar Jack was a pretty big fellow. He was a big man. When he was in working condition he weighed 325 pounds. A big moose of a fellow.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: He was really strong.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I say he was really strong. Yeah he was a strong man and big. Joe wasn't what you'd call a big man.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they come around together or what?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yeah. I've heard them talking about the two together. They used to run around together. Get drunk together.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This Cougar Jack, you know the story on how he got his name there? Called Cougar?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah I've heard that he was hauling card wood with his team in the sled and they had sled stakes to hold the card wood on that just fit in a stick pocket. And he killed a cougar with one of those sled stakes they said. And that's where he's supposed to have gotten his name. Cougar Jack.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Was he going to get in the address of somebody else who maybe knows about him?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes. I got an address of a woman and her sisters and brother but I never knew her. Georgia's sister. She went to school with one of the youngest boys. She went to school with him. And it tells about her in here. About the one that got killed over there in the mine. See that was just across the ridge here and there's gold mines.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know about the Micah Mountain?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: How did Micah come there?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I freighted there with the team and wagon. All the supplies up and the building material, all the Micah down. And my dad freighted there years ago. It was long about 1910 when he was hauled up there.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: They used to have a Micah shed up in Deary.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: During the war when they run those mines they used to cut the Micah up there. When they first started those mines before they ever had any road up there they used to pack that Micah out on packhorses before they got a road up there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it one man that had the mine there?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: There were several people that had mines in there. There were a great many different claims. They had what they called the Muscovite. It was the only one that ever really paid. It had the best quality Micah. Here's a list of all the different ones. Muscovite and the Bentz and the Wella, the Mabee, Levi Anderson, the Morning Star, the Sunshine, Avon. They had one mine they called the Avon mine. I didn't realize there were so many of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it easy to mine for?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well at first they were just pit mining, open pit mostly. And that's where they got the best Micah. It seems when it gets very much depth the pressure kind of shatters the Micah and it isn't clear. At first they had an open pit up there and they just got a lot of real good Micah. Great big books of it. The only time they've run it lately now is during the wartime when the government would pay a subsidy. But then is the only time they can afford to run it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there much of a market for it when they were first mining it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: When they first mined it, when they had the real good grade, there was a good market for it. The first automobiles that come out had the old side curtains and they had what they call icing glass. They'd split that thin and make the windows out of that. And then the heater stoves all had icing glass fronts on them, little windows so you could see the flames.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: They later used that Micah for, they re-mined them. All that stuff they pushed over and they...

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: And they also used it for axle grease. They had made real good axle grease when they had the wagons. Of course now then there's no demand for axle grease. And then I think they used it in some paints too of some kind.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did the mines employ many people up there working?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh they had, at first, quite a few men worked up there.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You mean by quite a few?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I suppose they had 25, probably 25 men or better up there when I first knew those mines.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: 25 for all of them?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: 25 for that Muscovite. And then of course the others had a few, but the Muscovite was the only one that ever really did pay.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Is that where you hauled from?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Uh huh.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were these miners just local fellows?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Most of them. Most were just local people from right around here… they..… there were some Englishmen that came in here, worked in the mines, that came here for that purpose. English miners at one time. But for the most part they were just the natives.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the social life like here you think in the early days? What social life?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yes, I think they had better times than you now.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, when I was small they had what they called literary societies. Of course they had the old schoolhouse. And every Saturday night they would have either a program of some description or else a debate. They would grate for debates. And they'd have debating teams and they would choose a subject one Saturday night for the following Saturday. And then they'd have debates. And of course have a big lunch and just an opportunity I think more to get together to visit than anything else.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: And high social?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: And then they had dances.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they have dances too in the schoolhouse when you were young?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I don't remember they ever had dances in the schoolhouse. They used to have dances in the homes. Where they had a big enough house where they'd have house parties and dances in the homes.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Dance all night.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: And sometimes they'd even stay for breakfast.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This when you first came here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah… during the Depression we had to furnish our own amusement then just the same as these early homesteaders did when they first came here.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Now this house when we first got it had halls to go clear around, a door, you could just make a big circle. It had musicians in one room and part of the time you couldn't hardly hear them but you'd just go around. They shut all the doors so they can't do that now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you saying that you had to depend on yourselves more during the Depression for entertainment than during the 20s before the Depression hit?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh yes. During the Depression you didn't have any money and you couldn't go anywhere or buy anything so we just had to furnish our own amusement. We had baseball teams and house parties and things of that kind that didn't take any money because we just didn't have any and no way to get any either.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: But people visited more locally than they do now. Now you get in a car and you go 100 miles.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: You want to see your neighbor now while you go to town. You see your neighbor on the street.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the Depression during those years, were they really hard years for people around here to get by or could you get by without any money okay by trading?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: You traded around the community and we all had lots to eat. Everybody had plenty to eat. You didn't have anything that took money. You'd get kind of ragged sometimes because you couldn't buy any clothes but everybody had plenty to eat. If one person had a surplus of one thing why they would trade with the neighbors and so everybody had plenty to eat.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Tell them about the trades. Tell them about the trades. Beans for beans.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh there were some farmers that farmed down here on Barrage and they raised a lot of beans in that country at that time. And so they couldn't sell their beans and they came up in this country trying to sell beans and come in here and wanted to sell me some beans. And I told them I don't have any money to buy beans but I said I've got some winter pigs. How about trading you some pigs for beans? Oh fine fine. They said we'll trade you straight across. Give you a sack of beans for a pig. Said how many pigs you got? Well I wound up I had 450 pounds of white beans. So we gave beans to the neighbors and we traded beans to the neighbors and I even sold some. I got 50 cents in cash for some beans.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How many pounds of sacks?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: They'd weigh about 120 pounds something like that. I'd give them a sack. But that's the only way they had to do at that time was the trade. We had lots of things to sell. We had hay to sell, grain, hogs, eggs, we sold cream and cattle but they didn't bring any money. I sold 200 pound hogs, fat hogs for five dollars apiece.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: They carried a five gallon can of cream from here to where the egg on is. On his back down there. Now I couldn't go down there and bring the empty can back.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: It snowed in here. See that was before the days of snow plowing. And they had horses and you just tramp the snow down. You pack it down. Then in the spring when it started to thaw, why horses couldn't travel because they'd break through and they just couldn't go. And it snowed in. We couldn't get out with the team. So I carried a five gallon can of cream from here down there. Got a dollar and fifty cents for it.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: When we first came in the winter time you could just take out across the country and go ride across the top of the fences and all with a team of horses and sleds. The snow was so deep. You don't have snow like that now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You really don't have the snow like that?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well you see there was no wind in this country because the timber was so heavy. And the snow would just come in the fall and just lay there. And now then we'll get a foot or so of snow and it'll thaw away and then we'll get some more. It'll do the same maybe a dozen times during the winter. But we had quite a few chickens during the depression and we sold eggs for a dollar? Seven cents a dozen. We had to pay twenty five cents for the case to put them in. Thirty dozen cases. We got seven cents a dozen for them.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: We never did see the man we sold them to. We sent them up on the train.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: All the money we had was we got the cream and a few eggs, things like that. Sold a few pigs. The price was so low.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: It was a good thing either. We could sell the cattle for them.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Eleven dollars. I sold yearlings for eleven dollars a head.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did a lot of people leave here during that time?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No. They moved from the towns out here. Every old shack that would hold people was occupied because they could live cheaper here than anywhere else. They just moved out here from anywhere they could find a place to live. A lot more people then than there is now.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: About every 40 acres is by that. You used to live on 40 acres. You can't do it now. We thought we'd retire when we got 200 acres in cultivation. But that time you got the machinery and you couldn't even buy the machinery to run up there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You were probably too young then to know what people were saying and thinking. But I imagine they must have foreseen that it was going to change the country a lot when it came through.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I suppose it did. It did change the country because the Potlatch started logging this timber and came in here with their camps and all the men. An awful lot of men in this country. It took so many more men to log then than it does now. I worked in camps that had way over 100 men in the camp. They had probably 12 or 14 different camps. Now then, I don't think there's over 100 men in the whole logging industry in this part of the country now. They must have had 10 times the men that they have now. It made a difference. Well, the trains used to be a day too. Yes, they had two passenger trains a day on this railroad. They only had two coaches. I rode that train more than once where you had to stand up. All the seats would be taken. That was the only way transportation had. You either rode the train or you walked one or the other.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well, now they just have a train every so often. I don't know how often it is, but it's a normal passenger train.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I have a freight train now about maybe two or three times a week. No. No, they got it for just almost nothing. They didn't know what timber they bought. Then of course they hired men to come in here and homestead too. Then the men would turn the land over to the Potlatch. Then the homesteaders that couldn't make a living on their land, they'd sell out to the Potlatch for a little or nothing. They got this land for just almost nothing. When they bought timber from the landowners, it was very, very low price. I don't know just what it was. But it wasn't very much.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They had guys homesteading right around in this country, right around here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I don't know here. I think it's more up around Bovill, up in that country, where they told me that they hired men to do homestead for them. Then they'd buy their rights as soon as they could prove up on it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did most of the guys living here start going to work in the camps then?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, oh yes, after the camps started. That's the way these little old stump ranchers, we'd call them, they'd have 40 or 80 acres and they'd work in the camps. That's the way they lived and then just gradually improved their places. They couldn't make a living on the places hardly because they wouldn't have enough land in cultivation.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, after they came in here, Potlatch, was this land still more used for grazing and for cattle than it was for just growing straight farm produce?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yeah, yes it was. I think, well I know there was more cattle in this country then than there is now. Every landowner had a few cattle and there were so many more people in there than there is now that there's more cattle raised here than there is at the present time. Because when we first came here, there was very little grain that was sold. It was all cattle and hay. They had a warehouse down here at Avon and that warehouse would just be piled with baled hay in the fall, just filled to the rafters. And then later years they wouldn't have any hay in it at all. It got to be all grain then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were the camps the main market for the cattle or did they get shipped out of the country some place like Lewiston?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well there would be cattle buyers come in here and buy the cattle and at first they used to drive them out before the days of trucks. They'd come in, buy up the cattle and drive them out to the, I don't know where they drove them, the railroads or where they drove them. And then after they got trucks, well then of course they trucked them more. But I can remember cattle buyers coming over to my granddad's in the fall and then he'd have maybe 30, 40 head of cattle to sell. They'd buy the whole bunch and just start down the road with them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know where they come from, these cattle buyers?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, I don't know where they came from. I don't know where they drove the cattle to. They must have driven them out to down Troy or some place, to the railroad I suppose and shipped them. I wouldn't have any idea. They'd almost have to ship them to Spokane.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the summer range for the cattle? Is there a lot of range that's shared by different people using it?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: It's all free range. There was no restrictions. Anybody that wanted to bring in cattle or anybody that owned cattle just turned them out. And they just had the run of the country. When we first came here, milk cows was the same way. Everybody had eight, ten milk cows and they'd milk them in the morning, turn them out on the road. At night, if they could find them, why they'd get them in and milk them. Sometimes they couldn't even find them. Free range.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where would they range mostly from around here? What would the range be? Would it be the woods and the hills? Would they use the meadows?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: The roads, they'd just run down the roads and then very little of this land was fenced. The only fences they'd have would be around the cultivated land. If you owned land that wasn't cultivated, why you didn't, most of them didn't even have a fence. And that was all open range.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of fencing did they use in the early days?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Early days was all rail fences. Split rail fences and then later they got wire, of course. But I never had any rail fences. After I came here, it was all wire. My granddad, he had his whole place fenced with rail fences, all his cultivated land.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've heard it said that there was a lot of, when the railroad came through that it really changed it. Like around here there was a lot of guys just working on the railroad, bunking in and things like that. There was a lot of gambling and drinking and the whole country was pretty wild and woolly for a period of time in there. Is that, do you learn to say anything?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, any country where there's those old lumberjacks and the old miners, I think was about the same. They were pretty wild, some of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you, were there many guys that would come by who were coming, like who had been riding the rails, who were tramps?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I don't know if you'd call them tramps. That's the way a lot of these old lumberjacks traveled. They just traveled a foot up and down the railroad track. And, oh, it would never be a day go by in the summertime if you didn't see somebody going a foot up that railroad track with a bedroll on his back. Going from one camp to another or else heading out towards town or either that or coming back from town after he'd went to town and spent all his money and come back broke and going back to the camps to go to work again. But there was a lot of that. People would just walk the railroad track.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there a big difference, you think, between the lumberjacks and the local boys like yourself who were working in the camps? As far as, oh, what would you do with your money?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes, I think there was. You know, these old lumberjacks, professional lumberjacks, they'd go and work in the camp maybe for three, four months or maybe longer and never get out of camp. Then they'd draw all their money and go to Spokane or Lewiston or someplace and in a week or ten days where they'd have it all spent and come back to camp sick and drunk and half drunk and sick and have to go back to work and make some more money and wouldn't have a cent left. And these local people around here, they all had these little places and probably a family on their places and they'd be out working in the camps and make money enough to live on during the winter or when they could stay home and work on their places. So they wouldn't go and blow their money like the old lumberjacks.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you think the local people in those days thought about Potlatch? You think they were more grateful for them for providing jobs and they were unhappy because they weren't paying money for timber? Was it a very mixed feeling?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I think so. I think there were a great many people of course that they were grateful for the chance to work and all that but at the same time they knew that they were being taken. You know, and I suppose it was more or less a mixed feeling.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: That time they worked their way around nothing anyway so they probably knew they were getting checked.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, would you tell me that story again about Arthur shooting a... Shooting a neighbor's cow. Yeah, I've heard that story before too. It's such a good one. Arthur's neighbors, they hunted together and lived right close together and they always hunted together and this neighbor had a cow that was in the pasture but the cow had gotten out of the pasture. And the neighbor's wife, she looked out and she saw this animal going down through the brush and she thought it was an elk. So she told her husband, they said, there goes an elk. And he said, well you call Arthur and tell him where to go and I'll go and see if I can chase it out to him. So Arthur went where they told him to go and he chased the cow out and Arthur shot it dead. Thought it was an elk.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long ago was this?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, that's...I suppose 15 years ago, something like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But he had a reputation for being a good hunter, didn't he?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, Arthur was a...he was the best shot I think in this whole country and a real good hunter. He was just a real good hunter. Here it tells in here about these old homesteaders. And he said, the government bet you 160 acres of land against $5 that you can't live on the land for five years without starving. That is about the truth too. Alright, thanks, I'm just going to go ahead and do this.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Cup of hot water drink, eh… thanks.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You're not putting me on that tape.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well it's hard not to get your voice on there too when you talk, so. I'm not going to do that. Not much he is on it.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: You don't have ... mouth, do you?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Matter of fact I do, but...

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: He's waiting for you to tell something about him.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Oh, well, I don't know what I can tell you about him. He was the general superintendent when I first started to work and then... I can't remember how many years he was there before Naugle took his place. A fellow by the name of Naugle became the superintendent then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you were growing up, besides the lumbering, the main work that you did?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Yes, when I first started to work out, I worked in the woods and then later I worked in construction work on government dams, some. But mainly woods work. There got to be several sawmills around the country and I worked on the dam too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you wind up starting to farm?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Long story.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: I worked in the woods and then I worked for the government building, construction, and then I went to work for my dad who had a general store about 30 miles this side of Spokane, a little town there. Then I bought an interest in that store. Then after a few years I got asthma and hay fever so bad that I had to get out of there. I didn't know where to go or what to do so I came back here where I was raised. Hay fever and asthma didn't bother me here so I came back here and there wasn't much else to do then but farm so I started in the farm. That's the reason I came back here, mainly on account of my health.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In the 20s?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: 1928. So you got into farming at a good time just before the depression. Yeah, just before the depression. We had about two or three years to get started before the depression hit.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: We bought all these farm equipment and we had the horses and everything. That's for $500. That's all we needed at that time. Later on, of course, we had to have a little fever.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you go in with and heard at farm as far as the amount of equipment? What did you have?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: We had four horses, harnessing, piles, harrows, drills, and hay machinery, mower and rake and so on. Everything, just about everything you needed to farm with. No, a lot. Really.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you need around here?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well, I lived in Helmer. I was a little kid then.

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Her dad was a logger too and I worked with him in the woods. I knew her when she wasn't very big yet.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: We moved to Spokane and then when he lived there in Fairfield, that's where the little place was. His dad had his job. Then he came up there and I stayed with him again. From there on, I left.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get married down here?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No. Well, I was still in Fairfield. We got married. We moved here right after. It wasn't very long afterward.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get shivareed when you got married or did you get around?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Three times.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Really?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: Three times. We got shivareed in Fairfield and then where she lived, at her home, then we came down here to visit. And this was shivareed. We got it again.Three different times.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: There were so many people here. I don't know where they came from or have any idea. But this house, as I told you, the doors, we had a door there and then we went in the next room and then come on around. And it was this standing room for people. I've never seen them before and I've never seen them since, some of them. I don't know who they were. I remember there was one blind lady and I was passing out candy bars. And I didn't know that she was blind. And somebody said, well, touch her on the hand. So I touched her hand and said, don't pick it up just like you can see. I don't know who she was or where she came from or anything. But they set off dynamite. We had these great big trees. I was told you noticed that big tree there on the corner. Well, all of this over here was over here was those great big trees. And there were two right out here that grew like this. They put the dynamite between the two, broke all of the windows on that side of the house. It cracked them. But anyway, we were shivering. I think it was just, I don't know. I guess that was the last one. And then, well, then my sister, she was married not too long afterwards. And they didn't break when we were shivering, but it cracked when she was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I think that's a custom. They shouldn't have given up.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: Well, sometimes they get carried away. They still, well, around here, they, you know, they, I don't know, just the last few years, I guess they haven't been reading people, have they?

segments.speaker: Kenneth Wilkins
segments.words: No, just the last few years.

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
segments.words: That's quite the thing. I was a bachelor at that time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think there was a very strong community here in your own days?

segments.speaker: Dorothy Wilkins
